how.heading: How it works
how.leadBefore: A slow, rate-limited API, made to feel instant. A chain of caches sits between you and NASA. Each layer only asks the next when it is
how.leadAfter: , and fills itself on the way back, so a request stops at the first warm layer.

steps.name: Vue Query
steps.desc: Holds a copy in your browser. A repeat view renders instantly, with no network at all. Invalidate it to force a fresh look at the server chain.

steps.name: Nitro
steps.desc: An in-process, in-memory stale-while-revalidate cache in front of Redis. A warm hit never leaves the server process, so it beats the Redis network hop; while fresh (30s) it answers directly, and once stale it serves the old value instantly AND refreshes in the background, so no request waits for a refresh. It doesn't survive serverless cold starts; then the request simply falls through to Redis.

steps.name: Redis
steps.desc: The persistent store, shared by every visitor and kept for 24 hours. A plain cache-aside store with no revalidation of its own: when an entry is gone, the next request blocks and refetches, which is exactly the wait that Nitro's SWR avoids. Nitro falls through to Redis on a miss.

steps.name: NASA APOD API
steps.desc: The single source of truth. Rate-limited and slow (the better part of a second per request), which is exactly why the caches exist.

how.guideLead: The controls in the footer work on every page. Here is what to watch.

guide.title: Read the chain
guide.desc: The footer shows the chain with a dot per layer; filled means that cache holds data. The badge on each card and the hero shows which layer is the current active source.

guide.title: Invalidate Vue Query
guide.desc: Revalidates the browser cache and refetches from the server chain: Nitro if warm, else Redis, else NASA. The footer reports the source and how long it took.

guide.title: Delete Nitro or Redis
guide.desc: Empties a server layer. The badge flips instantly to the next layer down. Delete both and the next request goes all the way to NASA: a genuine, rate-limited cold start.

how.scopeData: Every layer here caches data on its way from NASA to the page. The rendered HTML is a separate question, answered per route: the three static pages let the CDN serve them for an hour, while the APOD routes allow nothing and are rendered per request. A cached page could not honestly report which cache answered, because its labels would be as old as the copy. Route rules, prerendering and ISR are real and useful layers, just not the ones this project is about.
how.scopeBlueprint: The chain is also more elaborate than most projects need. A Nitro SWR cache in front of Redis earns its place here because you can watch a request stop at it and see what that saves; in production you would usually pick one server cache and move on. Read this as an X-ray of the layers, not as a blueprint to copy.

faq.heading: Questions about the cache
faq.lead: The short answers. The timeline on "How it works" has the long ones.

items.q: What was the motivation to build something like this?
items.a: A few years ago the idea of a server-side Redis cache came up in a Nuxt project I was working on. As an old-school frontend developer that layer had never been my problem, so I wanted to take one apart properly: what belongs in which cache, and what each layer actually buys you.

items.q: Why cache a public API at all?
items.a: NASA's APOD API is slow and rate-limited, and the gallery asks for 60 days at once. Cached, that becomes one request per day, served instantly to everyone after the first visitor.

items.q: What does each layer actually store?
items.a: All three store the same normalized APOD JSON: Vue Query in the browser and in localStorage, Nitro in the server process, Redis shared and persistent for 24 hours. The images are not in the chain. They ride the browser's HTTP cache and Netlify's Image CDN.

items.q: What is Vue Query, and what does it do here?
items.a: TanStack Vue Query is a data cache in the browser: one entry per query key, shared by every component that asks for it. Here it holds the APOD JSON under ["apod"] for the list and ["apod", date] for a single day, fresh for 24 hours, with no refetch on mount or window focus. The server passes its cache to the client in the page payload, so hydration costs no second request, and each entry is written to localStorage for repeat visits. It is the layer the footer's invalidate button acts on.

items.q: Is Vue Query actually needed here?
items.a: Yes, for the part that matters here. Nuxt's useAsyncData also carries server-fetched data into the client without a second request, but on an internal navigation it would fetch again: its default cache only reads the payload while hydrating, and Nuxt purges that data on navigation by design. Vue Query keeps one entry per key with a 24 hour stale time instead, so moving between the gallery, a picture and back costs no request at all. It also adds localStorage persistence and the invalidate API the footer button uses.

items.q: Why a Nitro cache and Redis? Isn't one enough?
items.a: For most projects one is enough. They are both here because they fail differently: a Nitro hit never leaves the server process and beats the Redis network hop, but it dies with the process and is not shared between instances. Redis survives both. Clear one in the footer and the request falls through to the other.

items.q: What is the difference between defineCachedFunction and defineCachedEventHandler?
items.a: Both come from Nitro rather than from Nuxt itself, and both have been available since Nuxt 3 (this project runs Nitro 2.13). They share the same options: maxAge, staleMaxAge, swr and getKey. defineCachedEventHandler caches a whole HTTP response for a route, keyed by the request, so on a hit the handler does not run at all. defineCachedFunction caches the return value of a single function, keyed by its arguments, and the handler around it still runs on every request.

items.q: Why does the Nitro layer cache a function here and not the route?
items.a: Because the response carries a flag saying which layer answered it, and that flag has to stay true. A cached event handler would serve the entire stored response, flag included, so the badge would claim Nitro forever and clearing Redis would change nothing on screen. Caching only the inner function keeps the handler running, so it can re-label every response. The event handler would work and would skip slightly more work per request, it just cannot report on itself, which is the same reason the HTML is not cached.

items.q: Why isn't the rendered HTML cached too?
items.a: The badges are written at render time, so a cached page would report a cache state as old as the copy. Route rules, prerendering and ISR are perfectly good tools; they just cache something else than this demo is about.

items.q: Why is the first load of a picture slow and the second instant?
items.a: Images are not part of the JSON chain. On first view Netlify's Image CDN fetches the NASA original and converts it to AVIF at the requested width; that conversion is the wait. Afterwards the variant is cached at the edge and in your browser.

items.q: How long does anything stay cached?
items.a: Redis 24 hours, for the list and for every single day. Nitro counts a value as fresh for 30 seconds and may then serve it stale for up to a day while it revalidates. Vue Query 24 hours in the browser. The daily miss is not a TTL: the list key contains its date range (last 60 days, ending yesterday), so at midnight it becomes a different key.

items.q: Would you build a production app exactly like this?
items.a: No: one server cache instead of two, and the HTML cached as well. The extra layers exist here to make the trade-offs visible and clickable.

about.heading: Making a slow API feel instant
about.lead1: A small side project about caching. The idea is simple: take NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day, a lovely but slow and rate-limited API, and see how instant it can feel with a couple of caches in front of it.
about.lead2: The browser never calls NASA directly. Requests flow through a chain of caches (Vue Query in the browser, a Nitro stale-while-revalidate cache and Redis on the server), each asking the next only when it is empty, and filling itself on the way back. Clear or invalidate any layer from the footer and watch where the next request really goes.
about.creditText: Built by Melanie Stief, who has always dreamed of flying to space, or at least working at NASA (which, sadly, will probably never happen in this lifetime).
